title: Wine Wimsey Review · Oct 31
subtitle: 16 feed (15 images + 1 TOBI at #8) and 4 stories · TOBI count: 1 because the posting date, Sat Oct 31, is a Saturday in even ISO week 44 · CHARACTER: The Hot Mess (single-character mode) · Inbox had no new items · Captions: 6 SHORT, 9 SEE MORE · EXPERIMENT posts: #10 neighbor-decorations bit, #11 witch-hat Halloween bit, #14 bank-teller vs app · Timely: Halloween night, and the TOBI is about clocks going back tonight · Credits: 19 images x ~45.3 = ~861 · FLAGGED: the WineWimsey stamp touches the last letters of the bottom text on #3 (COUCH.) and #5 (FORTY.), and lightly on #9, #10 and story 2; text stays readable, say the word and I will regenerate any of them

posts.quote: Nobody warns you that one day you'll love a coat purely for the pockets. Mine hold a tissue, a pen, and my whole personality.
posts.caption:
I have a coat I would run back into a burning building for. It isn't the color. It's the pockets, which are deep enough to lose a forearm in and have held, at various points, a tissue, a pen, a hair tie, and a grocery list from March.

I bought it at 4:10 on a Wednesday, on sale, and wore it out of the store with the tags still tucked in my sleeve. A woman in the next aisle asked where I found it. I said the back, like it was a secret. It still is.

Nothing else I own has been this loyal.
posts.first: I found a second hair tie behind the lining last week and felt like I'd been handed a small apology. The coat has been through two winters and one dry cleaner who looked at it for a long time. I picked it up the next day and we don't discuss it.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun standing in a hallway hugging a camel coat with her hands in its pockets and a glass of red wine on a table beside her. Text in the speech bubble reads: Nobody warns you that one day you'll love a coat purely for the pockets. Mine hold a tissue, a pen, and my whole personality.

posts.quote: I held the cereal box at arm's length, then at nose length, then gave up and bought it anyway. Surprise is a flavor.
posts.caption: The ingredients were printed somewhere between a whisper and a rumor. I gave it a real try, I want that on record. The cereal and I are now in a relationship based on trust.
posts.first: The glasses were on my head the entire time. I found them in the car and held them up to the windshield like evidence. Nobody was there to see it, which is the only reason I'm telling it now.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun squinting at a cereal box held at arm's length in a grocery aisle, a basket with lemons and a wine bottle on her arm. Text in the speech bubble reads: I held the cereal box at arm's length, then at nose length, then gave up and bought it anyway. Surprise is a flavor.

posts.quote: There is a version of me who got up at six and walked three miles. I wish her well from the couch.
posts.caption:
She has a good attitude and a matching set of workout clothes. I have seen her photos, mostly in other people's stories, mostly around 6:15 in the morning when I am negotiating with a pillow.

I don't resent her. We simply run different schedules, and by run I mean one of us does.

This morning I was up at 7:40 with a mug, a blanket, and a view of her getting smaller on the hill. I waved. I think she saw me. It felt like a good working relationship, honestly.
posts.first: My neighbor does the loop around the block every morning at 6:05. I know because the dog announces her. I used to feel bad about it. Now I time my coffee to her second lap, which feels like a partnership.
posts.alt: Painted cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun on a sofa under a patchwork blanket, mug in hand, waving at a tiny jogger on a hill outside a sunrise window. Text on the image reads: There is a version of me who got up at six and walked three miles. I wish her well from the couch.

posts.quote: My mother folded fitted sheets into perfect squares. I fold mine into a shape and close the closet door fast.
posts.caption:
My mother had a linen closet that looked like a store display. Every sheet set was squared off and labeled by room, and I have never once seen her stop to think about it. She just did it, the way other people breathe.

I've watched videos. I've pulled the corners. At 3:30 on a Saturday I once held a fitted sheet up like a patient on an operating table and said out loud, you win.

The folded shape goes on the shelf, the door shuts, and that is the whole system. Nobody has ever opened it to check.
posts.first: My mother's trick was something about tucking the corners inside each other. She showed me twice. I nodded both times and retained nothing. She brought it up at every holiday after that, with real affection, and I would nod again.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun holding a crumpled fitted sheet in a laundry room with a wine glass on the dryer behind her. Text on the image reads: My mother folded fitted sheets into perfect squares. I fold mine into a shape and close the closet door fast.

posts.quote: I arrived ten minutes early to the appointment. Now I've been nervous for forty.
posts.caption: The receptionist said the doctor was running behind. I said that's fine. It was not fine, it was a free trial of every thought I'd been avoiding. I read the same paragraph about a celebrity's kitchen eleven times.
posts.first: They called my name at 2:52. I stood up so fast the magazine hit the floor. The woman next to me gave me the look people give each other in situations like this. We did not say a word. It was a bond.
posts.alt: Comic panel illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun in a waiting room chair holding a clipboard, a wall clock and magazines behind her. Text on the image reads: I arrived ten minutes early to the appointment. Now I've been nervous for forty.

posts.quote: I counted my passwords. Eleven. I remember two, and one of them is wrong.
posts.caption: The website asked me to choose something I'd remember. I chose something I'd remember. It said I'd already used it, which means I once remembered it and then forgot it, which is the whole situation in one sentence.
posts.first: I keep a notebook with all of them. The notebook is somewhere in the house. It has a good hiding place, and I picked it myself, so of course I can't find it.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun at a desk in front of a laptop with sticky notes on the monitor and one on her cheek, a wine glass beside her. Text in the speech bubble reads: I counted my passwords. Eleven. I remember two, and one of them is wrong.

posts.quote: My hearing is fine. Everyone around me just took up mumbling around my fiftieth birthday.
posts.caption:
It started with the waiters. Then the pharmacy. Then my own family, who all seem to have picked up a habit of speaking toward their shoes.

I've asked what a few times and gotten the same answer at the same volume, which proves nothing except that they are consistent.

Last Sunday a man at the hardware store told me where the extension cords were. I nodded, walked to aisle nine, and came home with a lightbulb. It's a nice lightbulb, and I'd like to think it was meant to be. The extension cord is still on my list, written in handwriting I can read.
posts.first: My sister says I've been saying what since 2019. I told her that's not a long time. She said it's seven years. I said what. That was funny for about ten seconds, and then it was true.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun at a restaurant table cupping her ear toward a waiter, with bread and a wine glass on the table. Text in the speech bubble reads: My hearing is fine. Everyone around me just took up mumbling around my fiftieth birthday.

posts.quote: The clocks go back tonight. I plan to spend the extra hour exactly where I spend all the others, horizontal.
posts.first: Last year I set a reminder for it and slept through the reminder. The oven clock is still an hour off from March. I've decided that's a tradition at this point, and one the house seems to be keeping on my behalf.

posts.quote: I preheated the oven for a recipe I never started. It's the warmest the house has been all week.
posts.caption: The recipe called for 375 degrees and a good mood. I managed the first part. The oven doesn't judge, and the kitchen has never been nicer.
posts.first: Around 5:30 I put a sweater on over the sweater and sat on the floor in front of it. A plain Saturday. My knees creaked like a screen door and it was still the best seat in the house.
posts.alt: Comic panel illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun warming her hands at an open oven in a kitchen, with a cookbook, flour bag and wine glass on the counter. Text on the image reads: I preheated the oven for a recipe I never started. It's the warmest the house has been all week.

posts.quote: The neighbors have a twelve-foot skeleton and a fog machine. I have one cobweb and a porch light I'm not sure about.
posts.caption:
Every year the house across the street adds something. This year it's a skeleton taller than my garage, wearing a bathrobe. I respect the commitment. I also respect the electric bill, which I assume is theirs to explain.

My own display took eleven minutes. I bought the cobweb at the drugstore, and I stood back to admire it for a full thirty seconds before going inside.

It's understated. Some people call that effort, and I call it a position. It has held up fine so far, though a squirrel did sit on the cobweb for a while on Thursday.
posts.first: The skeleton's bathrobe was hung up on Thursday night and I saw it from the window. The man across the street was adjusting its slippers by flashlight. I closed the curtain, because some moments belong to the people in them.
posts.alt: Painted cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun on a modest porch with one small cobweb, looking across at a neighbor's house with a giant skeleton and fog, wine glass in hand. Text on the image reads: The neighbors have a twelve-foot skeleton and a fog machine. I have one cobweb and a porch light I'm not sure about.

posts.quote: My costume budget this year was a hat I already owned. I've been a witch for eleven years and nobody has complained.
posts.caption:
The hat lives on the shelf above the coats, next to a bag of dryer sheets that predates the hat. I take it down every October 31st, dust it off with my sleeve, and decide I'm done for the year.

It fits the way it fit in 2015. That's more than I can say for most things. A few kids stopped last year to ask if I was a real witch. I said that's for me to know, and shut the door gently. It was a very good exit, and I plan to use it again next year.
posts.first: The hat cost nine dollars at a drugstore in 2015. I've had it longer than some of my houseplants and every single one of them has died around it. It's been through more than the plants have. I think that's what they call durability.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun wearing a floppy black witch hat, smirking with a wine glass in hand and a small pumpkin at the bottom. Text on the image reads: My costume budget this year was a hat I already owned. I've been a witch for eleven years and nobody has complained.

posts.quote: A stranger called me ma'am in the checkout line and held the door. I think I've been promoted.
posts.caption:
He was maybe thirty, with a nice jacket and a bag of oranges. He said after you, ma'am, and held the door like it was a coat check. I thanked him in a normal voice and walked three steps before thinking about it.

Then I thought about it for the rest of the evening. I put the groceries away with a new posture. I checked the mirror twice.

The oranges were a good choice, by the way. I bought a bag of my own on the way out, to feel part of something.
posts.first: A friend called to ask about dinner and I said I'd been promoted. She asked to what. I said ma'am. She laughed for a while, and then she said that's not a promotion. I said it comes with a door held open, so I'm keeping it.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun at a grocery checkout looking pleasantly surprised, with a wine bottle and bread on the conveyor belt. Text in the speech bubble reads: A stranger called me ma'am in the checkout line and held the door. I think I've been promoted.

posts.quote: My mother raked leaves in a skirt and never broke a sweat. I rake in a vest and negotiate with every bag.
posts.caption:
She wore a belted skirt, a cardigan, and small shoes, and the leaves just sort of went where she told them. I remember the sound of the rake, even and patient, and the neat pile at the end.

I go out at 2:30 with every good intention. By 2:45 the bag has collapsed twice and I've said something to it that I would not say to a person.

The yard looks fine from the road. That's the standard I've settled on, and I'm told the neighbors are comfortable with it. At least nobody has said otherwise to my face, and the leaf bag stays quiet.
posts.first: My mother never owned a leaf blower. She said it was louder than the problem. I bought one in 2021 and it has been in the garage ever since, still in the box. I tell people it's saving itself for a bigger occasion.
posts.alt: Painted cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun in an autumn backyard struggling with a floppy leaf bag, a rake against a tree and a wine glass on a stump. Text on the image reads: My mother raked leaves in a skirt and never broke a sweat. I rake in a vest and negotiate with every bag.

posts.quote: The bank teller asked if I'd like to use the app. I said I'd like to use the teller. We both had a moment.
posts.caption: She was kind about it. She said the app takes ninety seconds. I said so does standing here, and I did, while she stamped my slip with real feeling.
posts.first: She remembered my name at the end. I hadn't told her. It was on the slip, but still. I walked out slowly, enjoying the moment, and then sat in the parking lot for a little while thinking about the app.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun at a bank teller window holding a deposit slip and a phone, with a smiling teller behind the glass. Text in the speech bubble reads: The bank teller asked if I'd like to use the app. I said I'd like to use the teller. We both had a moment.

posts.quote: I put on the good jeans to see if they still fit. They do. Sitting is a separate conversation.
posts.caption:
I found them in the back of the closet behind a sweater I've been meaning to donate since 2022. They buttoned on the first try, and for four seconds I felt like a woman who'd won something.

Then I sat down on the edge of the bed to put on my shoes, and the jeans had thoughts about it.

They look great standing up. I've decided that's a full outfit, and I'll be standing at the party, near a wall, with a plate held at chest height. It's a plan, and I've made worse ones.
posts.first: I wore them to the store and stood in every aisle with excellent posture. In the car I undid the button, and the relief was so complete that I forgave them everything. We're still on good terms, though I've set some boundaries.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun in front of a bedroom mirror in dark jeans with a hand on her waistband, a wine glass on the dresser behind her. Text in the speech bubble reads: I put on the good jeans to see if they still fit. They do. Sitting is a separate conversation.

posts.quote: I carry a purse the size of a carry-on. It holds a spoon, two umbrellas, and no keys.
posts.caption: The spoon has been in there since a yogurt in August. The umbrellas were for two different rainstorms. The keys are somewhere, and I can feel them, which is not the same as having them.
posts.first: I turned the bag upside down in the driveway on Tuesday and the keys fell out last, as if they'd been waiting for an audience. They landed in a puddle. I picked them up and looked at the sky for a while.
posts.alt: Cartoon illustration of a woman with a messy grey-streaked bun emptying an enormous purse onto a hallway table, with a spoon, two umbrellas and receipts spilling out and a wine glass nearby. Text in the speech bubble reads: I carry a purse the size of a carry-on. It holds a spoon, two umbrellas, and no keys.
